reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard immunology references
clinicalPearls: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder of lysosomal trafficking caused by mutations in the LYST gene
The diagnostic morphological clue is giant cytoplasmic granules in neutrophils and other leucocytes seen on the blood film
Patients have partial oculocutaneous albinism with silvery hair and photophobia, reflecting abnormal melanosome function
Recurrent pyogenic infections, especially with Staphylococcus aureus and other bacteria, arise from impaired neutrophil chemotaxis, degranulation, and killing
Natural killer cell and cytotoxic T-cell function is defective, contributing to both infection risk and the tendency to develop an accelerated inflammatory phase

The dreaded 'accelerated phase' is a haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis-like syndrome with fever, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and lymphohistiocytic infiltration, often triggered by viral infection such as EBV
A progressive neurological syndrome (peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, cognitive decline) may emerge in those who survive childhood

Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can correct the immune and haematological disease but does not reverse the neurological degeneration; supportive care includes infection prophylaxis and treatment of the accelerated phase
reference.pathophysiology: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is caused by biallelic mutations in LYST, which encodes a protein regulating the size and trafficking of lysosomes and related organelles. Defective vesicle fusion produces the characteristic giant granules and disrupts the function of cells that depend on regulated secretory lysosomes, including neutrophils (impaired chemotaxis and delayed bacterial killing), cytotoxic lymphocytes and natural killer cells (defective granule-mediated cytotoxicity), melanocytes (partial albinism), and neurons. The failure of cytotoxic cells to control activated immune cells underlies the life-threatening accelerated phase resembling haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, while accumulation of abnormal lysosomal material contributes to the progressive neurodegeneration.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (familial HLH, EBV-driven HLH)
Leukocyte adhesion deficiency and other neutrophil disorders
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood film and bone marrow to identify giant granules in leucocytes
Neutrophil function testing (chemotaxis and bactericidal activity)
Natural killer and cytotoxic T-cell function assays
Markers of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (ferritin, soluble IL-2 receptor, triglycerides, fibrinogen) when the accelerated phase is suspected
Neurological assessment including nerve conduction studies
redFlags: Features of the accelerated phase (fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, hyperferritinaemia) requiring urgent HLH-directed treatment
Recurrent or severe pyogenic infection requiring prompt immunological evaluation
Live vaccines should be avoided given the cytotoxic immune defect
Irradiated, leucodepleted blood products are advisable, particularly around transplantation
Progressive neurological deterioration signalling advanced disease
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is guarded: most patients enter the accelerated phase in childhood, which is frequently fatal without treatment, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, if performed before this phase, can restore immune and haematological function but does not prevent the later progressive neurological decline.
pitfalls: Missing the giant leucocyte granules on the blood film and delaying diagnosis
Failing to recognise and aggressively treat the accelerated phase as an HLH-like emergency
Assuming transplantation will halt the neurodegeneration
Overlooking the albinism and hair colour clues that point to the diagnosis
Not screening for EBV or other viral triggers that can precipitate the accelerated phase
